Chapter 4: Facing Racism, Violence, and the Limits of Belonging.
As the boy starts to leave childhood behind and step into adolescence, the realities of racism can’t be ignored anymore. Suddenly, all those rules that once felt random—they start to make sense, in a way that’s hard to stomach. Their real purpose? To keep people in their place, enforcing inequality at every turn. He begins to notice how even the smallest acts of independence—standing a little taller, speaking up, or just meeting someone’s gaze—can trigger suspicion or even outright hostility. Imagine not being able to look someone in the eye without worrying it’ll be seen as a challenge. That’s the world he’s navigating.
Work introduces a whole new set of lessons. The boy takes jobs in white households and businesses, where the expectations are crystal clear: keep your head down, stay quiet, try not to be seen. Any hint of pride or intelligence? That’s met with anger—or worse, ridicule. So, the boy learns to hide, putting on a mask of compliance just to get through the day. But that comes at a cost. Each shift brings fresh humiliation, more reminders that, in their eyes, he’s less than fully human.
And then there’s the threat of violence—always lurking nearby. He sees beatings, hears threats, and lives with the constant fear that one wrong move could end in disaster. Watching adults around him swallow their anger and accept injustice just to survive, he feels the pressure to do the same. But deep down, he can’t. Something inside him refuses to accept a world where dignity is denied and fear rules every day.
There’s some comfort in the community, but it comes with its own set of rules. He’s expected to fit in, stay under the radar, and accept the limits society imposes. It’s a strange push and pull—feeling both a part of this world and somehow apart from it. He craves connection, but even more, he longs for freedom. That tension between belonging and independence? It shapes everything.
Religion weaves through it all in complicated ways. His grandmother and mother lean on faith, finding comfort and resilience in their beliefs. For the boy, though, religion feels like another set of boundaries, another way to control what he thinks and how he acts. He respects the peace it brings his family, but he knows his own search for meaning has to come from within.
As he grows, he becomes more aware of the heavy psychological toll that racism and poverty take. He sees how fear and anger shape lives, how dreams are quietly crushed before they even have a chance. The weight of expectations presses in—from the world outside and from his own community. The struggle to find where he belongs, to claim a sense of self, becomes more urgent every day.
And yet, he refuses to give in. He keeps reading, writing, and dreaming of something more. He searches for others who share his hunger for change—people willing to question the world as it is. Some days, the journey feels lonely, but he draws strength from knowing he’s not alone.
The fight for dignity, for freedom, for a voice of his own—this becomes his life’s true struggle.
